bib.title: Chapter 8. Patterns to Make the Most of LLMs (Learning LangChain)

question: How can an LLM application be designed to push out the agency-reliability frontier despite LLM limitations?
contributions: Frames agency vs reliability as a frontier and lists latency, autonomy and variance as competing objectives
Four techniques: structured output, streaming/intermediate output, human-in-the-loop controls, and double-texting (concurrency) modes

results.claim: Agency and reliability trade off along a frontier; chains sit at lower agency and higher reliability, agents at higher agency and lower reliability.
results.quote: notice how the chain architecture has relatively low agency but higher reliability, whereas the Agent architecture has higher agency at the expense of lower reliability.

results.claim: Human-in-the-loop controls can make high-agency architectures reliable.
results.quote: which can often make the difference in making high-agency ar‐
results.note: Sentence continues on next line: 'chitectures reliable.'

limits: No experiments or measurements; every statement is design guidance.
Code is LangGraph/LangChain specific (MemorySaver, interrupt_before, update_state, get_state_history); APIs may have changed since 2025.
Double-texting strategies are described only in prose; the chapter says some are implemented in LangGraph Platform (Chapter 9).
practices: Use low temperature for structured output to reduce invalid, schema-nonconforming output (Structured Output).
Give every schema field a description, since the LLM uses name plus description to decide what goes where (Structured Output).
Prefer tool calling or JSON mode over prompting alone for format; prompting is a suggestion, not a guarantee (Structured Output).
Stream node-level updates (stream_mode updates/values/debug) to make multi-step latency tolerable (Intermediate Output).
Attach a checkpointer so state persists per thread_id; all human-in-the-loop modes depend on it (Human-in-the-Loop).
Use interrupt_before on tool nodes to implement authorize-before-tool-call (Human-in-the-Loop).
Resume with None input, restart with new input, edit with update_state, fork by replaying get_state_history (Human-in-the-Loop).
Use UUIDs as thread IDs; a new thread_id discards state.
Mix human-in-the-loop controls to suit the application.

For concurrent input, fork-and-merge is likely best if state is mergeable (e.g. CRDTs) or the user resolves conflicts; otherwise choose among refuse, independent, queue, interrupt (Multitasking LLMs).
When keeping partial state after an interrupt, clean up dangling tool-call messages or the run may be unable to progress (Interrupt).
